note.question: What determines the economic and environmental implications of jointly implementing leasing and modularity, two prominent circular economy strategies, and their interaction?
note.overview: We investigate the economic and environmental implications of jointly implementing leasing and modularity, two prominent circular economy strategies, and their interaction. The paper develops a durable goods model to obtain insights for firms considering the use of these strategies. We first analyze the effect of adopting leasing on a firm’s product architecture choice.

Accordingly, ﬁrms may ﬁnd leasing more proﬁtable because it allows them to remove off-lease products from the consumer market, reducing the cannibalization of new products (Waldman 1997, 2003; Desai and Purohit 1998, 1999; Hendel and Lizzeri 1999b).

The ﬁrm can design its product with an integral or a modular architecture.

Building on these results, we show that leasing a modular product is preferred by the firm only under limited conditions (i.e., when production costs are low, off-lease products are in relatively better condition, and when there is a large difference between depreciation levels of different modules).
Consequently, a stream of papers in this literature focuses on identifying market structure and product characteristics under which selling can be more proﬁtable than leasing.

In contrast, the modules are decoupled under a modular architecture, enabling the firm or the customers to replace the modules independently.

Under selling, the firm sells the modules independently of each other, and customers can choose to replace only one of the modules of their existing product (in addition to retaining or replacing both modules) and sell the used modules on the secondary market.

Third, when the off-lease products are in a better condition (i.e., γ > 1), leasing a modular product becomes more attractive for a larger differential in the durabilities of the modules (see discussion of Lemma 2).

Modularity makes leasing less attractive when the off-lease products depreciate to a greater extent (γ < 1): that is, the cost threshold for leasing to be more profitable than selling is lower under a modular architecture (CM(δ1, δ2, γ) < CI(δ1, δ2, γ) for γ < 1).
